title: The true scholar
hookLine: the true pandit is one who instructs his own mind

lines: WHO DOES THE PANDIT TEACH FIRST?
cards: A friend can win any argument and still can't stop checking his phone at dinner. A brilliant expert gives wonderful advice and never takes any of it.
A teacher explains patience beautifully and loses her temper at the photocopier. Knowing a lot and being changed by what you know are two very different things.
In the Guru's day, the pandit was the learned one, the scholar who knew the old texts and taught them. Ashtpadi nine asks: who does the true pandit teach first?

teach.h: SO PANDIT: HE TEACHES HIS OWN MIND.
teach.b: The stanza opens: so pandit jo man parbodhai. That one is a pandit who instructs his own mind. Parbodh means to awaken, to teach, to bring to understanding.
The first student is the self.
Next: he searches for the Lord's Name within his own soul. Then: he drinks the sweet essence of the Name, and by that pandit's teaching the world lives.
And a line that shows this pandit isn't rejecting learning: he understands the root of the old scriptures, and sees the large hidden in the small.
So the true scholar still reads, but the reading has gone inward first and come back out as a life.
Then a line with real weight in a society ordered by caste: he gives teaching to all four castes. Chahu varnaa: all four. The stanza's ideal scholar teaches everyone.
Sikh practice carries that on: the Guru Granth Sahib, written in Gurmukhi script in the spoken languages of its time, is read aloud to anyone who walks into the gurdwara.
The stanza ends with Nanak bowing, forever, to that kind of pandit.

teach.h: INWARD FIRST, THEN OUT AS A LIFE.
teach.b: So the order matters: teach your own mind first, and then your teaching might keep the world alive.
This isn't anti-intellectual. Sikh tradition honors its scholars, poets and scribes. It's about which direction the learning flows.

how: Sikhs value study of Gurbani through katha and personal reading, and read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that learning should first change the learner.

o: a singer who leads hymns in the gurdwara
a scholar whose learning starts within
a teacher paid to explain the old texts

games.q: the true scholar — tap the pairs.

s: the stanza tells Sikhs to stop reading scripture
the true pandit understands the root of the old scriptures; the reading goes inward first.
the true pandit, in the stanza, teaches all four castes
teaching for everyone, not one group.
the stanza ends with Nanak bowing to that kind of pandit

games.q: you're the learned one in your village. by ashtpadi nine, who do you teach first?
games.why: so pandit jo man parbodhai: the pandit is the one who instructs his own mind, and then teaches all four castes.

practice: Pick a piece of advice you often give other people, slow down, drink water, don't take it personally, and say it now, silently, to yourself, as both the teacher and the student.
Then ask your mind, kindly, did you hear that, and sit with the answer without scolding. If you pray, you can ask for an awakened mind.

wordCard.voice: Pandit, a learned person. So pandit jo man parbodhai: the real pandit is the one who instructs his own mind, and then teaches everyone.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pandit, a learned person; ashtpadi nine names the true one as the one who teaches his own mind.

carryVoice: Your line: teach your own mind. The first student is always the self. That's day four hundred seventy-one.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
